summaryEn: Taiwan's largest industrial motor maker, founded in 1956, now selling power and cooling systems into AI data centres — where its chairman says orders are doubling and the only constraint is capacity. Earnings have nonetheless declined three years running, and the shares trade at 28 times them.
model: editorial (truth-audited: FinMind + earnings call coverage; motors framing — the +30% power-group growth, the Dynaciate acquisition, the guided +20%/+50% motor order growth and the AI datacentre pipeline credited, but the central tension stated plainly: EPS has fallen 2.77 → 2.73 → 2.42 across three years, FY2025 revenue rose 7% while EPS fell about 11%, trailing ROE is 6.24%, the dividend was cut from NT$2.2 to NT$2.0, and the stock trades at 28× those declining earnings; US contribution not expected before 2027; sector 電機機械 → Electric Motors & Power Systems)

sections.bodyMarkdown:
TECO Electric & Machinery (東元電機, TWSE: 1504) has been making electric motors since **1956**. It is Taiwan's largest industrial motor manufacturer, **listed since 1973**, and it also makes air conditioning, home appliances, electrical infrastructure and electric-vehicle powertrains. For most of seventy years it was a solid, unglamorous supplier of the machinery that makes factories turn.

Then AI data centres arrived, and TECO found itself selling into one of the fastest-growing capital-spending cycles in modern industry. Data centres need **power distribution, transformers, switchgear, motors and enormous amounts of cooling** — precisely TECO's product set. The evidence of the shift is real: **2026Q1 revenue in the power and energy business group rose more than 30% year-on-year**, the company approved the **acquisition of Malaysia's Dynaciate Engineering in May 2026** to build modular data centre capability, and chairman **Lee Ming-hsien** has described orders as doubling with capacity the only constraint. Management guides **high-voltage motor orders up about 20%** and **Taiwan high-efficiency motor orders up about 50%**, expects **FY2026 gross margin above FY2025's 23.8%**, and is in discussions on US data centre work that would contribute **from 2027 at the earliest**.

**And yet none of it has reached the bottom line.** Annual EPS has **declined three years running: NT$2.77 (FY2023) → 2.73 (FY2024) → NT$2.42 (FY2025)**. FY2025 revenue rose about **7% to NT$59.09bn** while EPS fell roughly **11%**. **2026Q1 EPS of NT$0.51 was below the NT$0.54 of a year earlier.** Gross margin has been flat at **23–25%** for six quarters, operating margin has oscillated between **6.5% and 11.2%**, and **trailing return on equity is 6.24%** — low for a company with **NT$90.7bn of equity**. The dividend was **cut from NT$2.2 to NT$2.0**.

The balance sheet is not the issue: **NT$143.2bn of assets, NT$90.7bn of equity, a conservative 36.6% debt ratio and NT$27.6bn of cash**, with **operating cash flow of NT$1.21bn broadly matching NT$1.24bn of net income**. The issue is the price. At **NT$63.00 the shares trade at 28× earnings and 1.76× book** — a growth multiple applied to earnings that have gone backwards for three years.

The honest read: **a real, verifiable AI data centre order story attached to a company whose profits have not yet moved — where the entire investment case is that they are about to.**

TECO was founded in **1956**, when Taiwan was electrifying and industrialising simultaneously. Its product was the **electric motor** — the device that converts electricity into rotation, and therefore the thing that actually does the work in almost every factory, pump, fan, compressor, lift and conveyor ever built. A country building an industrial base needs motors in enormous quantity, and TECO built them.

It **listed in 1973**, and expanded outward from motors along two logical paths. The first was **electrical infrastructure**: transformers, switchgear, drives and the systems that get power from the grid to the machine. The second was **appliances and air conditioning** — the same electromechanical competence applied to consumer and commercial products, giving TECO a household brand alongside its industrial one. Later it added **electric vehicle powertrains**, which are, at their core, motors and control electronics.

For decades this was a mature business: steady, cyclical with industrial capital spending, well capitalised, and not growing much. Annual earnings hovered in a narrow band, the dividend was reliable, and the company was regarded as a proxy for Taiwanese industrial activity rather than a growth story.

What changed was where electricity is now being consumed. An **AI data centre is, industrially, a very large electrical and thermal problem**: bringing tens or hundreds of megawatts in, distributing and conditioning it, and removing the heat that results. That requires **transformers, switchgear, power distribution, chillers, pumps, fans and motors** — TECO's catalogue, at unprecedented scale. The company has moved deliberately to serve it, including **acquiring Malaysia's Dynaciate Engineering in 2026** to offer modular data centre solutions, and pursuing work across Taiwan, Southeast Asia and eventually the United States.

It is a genuine second act for a seventy-year-old company. Whether it becomes a financial one is, so far, an open question.

- **1956 (12 June)** — TECO Electric & Machinery founded, making electric motors for Taiwan's industrialisation.
- **1973 (5 Nov)** — **Lists on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (1504)**.
- **1970s–2000s** — Expands from motors into **electrical infrastructure, air conditioning and home appliances**; builds international operations.
- **2010s** — Adds **electric-vehicle powertrains**, applying motor and drive expertise to automotive electrification.
- **2022** — **FY2022 EPS NT$1.64**; dividend NT$1.5.
- **2023** — Best recent year: **FY2023 EPS NT$2.77**; dividend raised to **NT$2.2**.
- **2024** — **FY2024 EPS NT$2.73**; dividend held at **NT$2.2**; gross margin around 25%.
- **2025** — Revenue rises about **7% to NT$59.09bn**, but **FY2025 EPS falls to NT$2.42** and the **dividend is cut to NT$2.0**; gross margin **23.8%** for the year.
- **2026Q1** — **Power and energy business group revenue up more than 30% year-on-year**; consolidated revenue **NT$14.24bn**; **EPS NT$0.51** against NT$0.54 a year earlier.
- **2026 (April)** — Monthly revenue of **NT$5.63bn**, up **13.55%** year-on-year — the second-highest month on record.
- **2026 (May)** — Board approves the **acquisition of Malaysia's Dynaciate Engineering** for AI data centre and modular data centre capability. Chairman **Lee Ming-hsien** describes orders as doubling with capacity the constraint; guidance for **high-voltage motor orders +20%**, **Taiwan high-efficiency motor orders +50%**, and FY2026 gross margin above **23.8%**. US data centre work expected to contribute **from 2027 at the earliest**.

TECO's accounts describe **a well-capitalised industrial company with a compelling order narrative and declining profits**.

- **Earnings have fallen three years running.** Annual EPS: **NT$1.64 (FY2022) → 2.77 (FY2023) → 2.73 (FY2024) → NT$2.42 (FY2025)**, with **2026Q1 at NT$0.51 against NT$0.54** a year earlier. This is the single most important fact about the company, and it sits directly against the growth narrative.
- **Revenue grew while profit shrank.** FY2025 revenue rose about **7% to NT$59.09bn** while EPS fell roughly **11%**. Growth is being bought at lower margin, at least so far.
- **Margins have not moved.** Gross margin: **25.3% (2024Q4) → 24.2% → 23.5% → 24.4% → 23.3% → 23.5% (2026Q1)** — flat within a narrow band for six quarters. Operating margin has ranged **6.5% to 11.2%** with no trend. Management guides **FY2026 gross margin above FY2025's 23.8%**; that has not yet appeared.
- **Return on equity is the weak point.** **6.24% trailing**, on **NT$90.7bn of equity**. For comparison, several manufacturers in this collection earn two to three times that on far less capital. A large, under-worked balance sheet is the structural issue behind the valuation question.
- **The balance sheet itself is excellent.** **NT$143.2bn of assets** against **NT$90.7bn of equity** — a conservative **36.6% debt ratio** — with **NT$27.6bn of cash**. **2026Q1 operating cash flow of NT$1.21bn** essentially matched **NT$1.24bn of net income**, so the earnings that exist are real cash.
- **The dividend was cut.** Cash dividends (FinMind, by fiscal year): **NT$1.15 (2020) → 1.35 → 1.5 → NT$2.2 (2023) → 2.2 (2024) → NT$2.0 (2025)**. The **3.17% yield** at NT$63.00 follows the earnings down.
- **The valuation is the crux.** **28× earnings and 1.76× book** for a company earning **6.24% on equity** with **three consecutive years of declining EPS**. The multiple prices the AI data centre order book, not the results.

The financing reality: **a financially sound company with plenty of capacity to invest, whose profitability has been going the wrong way while its order commentary has been going the right way.**

**Stance: a verifiable AI data centre order story — power group revenue +30%, orders described as doubling, a Malaysian acquisition for modular data centres — attached to a company whose EPS has fallen three years running and which trades at 28x those earnings.**

The bull case:

1. **The AI data centre opportunity fits the catalogue exactly.** A data centre is an electrical and thermal problem at industrial scale: **transformers, switchgear, power distribution, chillers, motors and cooling**. TECO has made all of it for seventy years, and the **power and energy business group grew revenue more than 30%** in 2026Q1.
2. **Concrete actions, not just commentary.** The **May 2026 acquisition of Malaysia's Dynaciate Engineering** adds modular data centre capability; guidance is for **high-voltage motor orders +20%** and **Taiwan high-efficiency motor orders +50%**; and management expects **FY2026 gross margin above 23.8%**. Chairman **Lee Ming-hsien** has said the constraint is capacity, not orders.
3. **Financial capacity to execute.** **NT$27.6bn of cash**, a **36.6% debt ratio** and **NT$90.7bn of equity** — ample room to invest in the capacity the chairman says is missing.
4. **A geographic pipeline.** Taiwan and Southeast Asia now; US data centre discussions contributing **from 2027 at the earliest**.

The counter-arguments:

- **Three consecutive years of falling EPS.** **NT$2.77 → 2.73 → NT$2.42**, and **2026Q1 below the prior year**. The order story has been told for some time; the profits have not followed.
- **Revenue grew 7% while EPS fell 11%** in FY2025 — growth at declining margin.
- **Margins are flat.** Gross margin has sat at **23–25%** for six quarters despite the mix shift.
- **Return on equity of 6.24%** on a large capital base — and **28× earnings** for that.
- **The dividend was cut** from NT$2.2 to NT$2.0.

An **anticipation** thesis: everything depends on the order book converting into margin. Until gross margin and EPS move, the multiple is paying for a future that has not arrived.

TECO sells **machines that use or manage electricity**, across four related areas:

- **Industrial motors (the historical core).** Motors that drive pumps, fans, compressors, conveyors and machine tools — sold to industrial customers, utilities and OEMs worldwide. Demand tracks industrial capital spending. Guidance is for **high-voltage motor orders up about 20%** and **Taiwan high-efficiency energy-saving motor orders up about 50%**, the latter driven by efficiency regulation and electricity costs.
- **Power and energy systems (the growth engine).** Transformers, switchgear, drives and electrical infrastructure — increasingly sold into **data centres**, where getting tens of megawatts safely from the grid to the racks is a substantial engineering project. This group's revenue rose **more than 30% year-on-year** in 2026Q1, and it is where the AI story lives.
- **Air conditioning and cooling.** Chillers and HVAC — historically commercial and residential, now also relevant to data centres, which must remove essentially all the power they consume as heat.
- **Home appliances and EV powertrains.** A consumer brand business, and an automotive electrification business applying the same motor and drive competence.
- **The data centre proposition, assembled.** By combining power distribution, cooling and now — through the **Dynaciate acquisition** — modular data centre engineering, TECO can sell a package rather than components. That is a higher-value position, and it is the strategic logic of the acquisition.

The economics are **industrial equipment economics**: gross margin around **23–25%**, operating margin in the high single digits to low teens, and profitability driven by **mix, utilisation and project execution**. The strength is a genuine product fit with the largest capital-spending cycle in the industry, backed by **NT$27.6bn of cash** to fund capacity.

The weakness is visible in the same numbers: **gross margin has not moved in six quarters** despite the mix shift, and **return on equity is 6.24%** on **NT$90.7bn of equity**. Selling more into data centres has, so far, grown revenue without improving the return — which is the question the company has to answer.

Electrical equipment has become, unexpectedly, an AI industry.

- **Why data centres are an electrical problem.** A large AI data centre draws power measured in **hundreds of megawatts**. Delivering it requires substation-scale transformers, medium- and low-voltage switchgear, distribution, backup and protection. Almost all of that power becomes **heat**, which must be removed by chillers, pumps and air handling. None of this is novel technology — it is conventional electrical and mechanical engineering at unusual scale and on unusual timelines.
- **The bottleneck is manufacturing capacity, not design.** Global demand for **transformers and switchgear** has outrun supply, with lead times stretching. This is the same dynamic visible at **Fortune Electric (1519)** elsewhere in this collection, whose share price re-rated dramatically on it — and TECO's chairman describing capacity rather than orders as the constraint is the same observation.
- **The competitive set.** Globally, **Siemens, ABB, Schneider Electric, Eaton and Hitachi Energy** dominate large electrical infrastructure; **WEG, Nidec and Toshiba** compete in motors. In Taiwan, TECO competes with **Fortune Electric, Shihlin Electric and Chung-Hsin Electric**. TECO's differentiation is breadth — motors, power systems and cooling from one supplier — plus the Southeast Asian footprint the Dynaciate acquisition strengthens.
- **Where TECO sits versus its Taiwanese peers.** Several Taiwanese electrical companies have participated in this cycle; the market has generally rewarded the ones with the most concentrated exposure. TECO's exposure is **diluted by appliances, air conditioning and general industrial motors** — which makes it less of a pure play, and helps explain why its aggregate earnings have not moved while its power group grew 30%.
- **The efficiency regulation tailwind.** Rising electricity costs and efficiency standards push industrial users toward **high-efficiency motors**, which is why Taiwan orders in that category are guided up about **50%**.

TECO's position is **broad rather than sharp**. The industry truth is that **the AI electrical boom rewards concentration** — a company where data centres are most of the business sees it in the results; a company where they are one growing segment among many sees it in the commentary.

**Strengths**
- **Seventy years of electrical and motor engineering**; Taiwan's largest industrial motor maker.
- **Product fit with AI data centres**: power distribution, transformers, switchgear, chillers and cooling; **power group revenue +30% YoY**.
- **Dynaciate Engineering acquisition (May 2026)** adding modular data centre capability in Southeast Asia.
- **Strong balance sheet**: **36.6% debt ratio**, **NT$27.6bn cash**, **NT$90.7bn equity**; operating cash flow matches net income.

**Weaknesses**
- **EPS declined three years running**: **NT$2.77 → 2.73 → NT$2.42**; 2026Q1 below prior year.
- **FY2025 revenue +7% while EPS fell ~11%** — growth at lower margin.
- **Gross margin flat at 23–25%** for six quarters; **operating margin 6.5–11.2%** with no trend.
- **Trailing ROE 6.24%** on a large capital base; **dividend cut from NT$2.2 to NT$2.0**.

**Opportunities**
- **High-voltage motor orders guided +20%**, Taiwan high-efficiency motors **+50%**.
- Southeast Asian and Taiwanese data centre projects; **US contribution from 2027** at the earliest.
- Management guidance for FY2026 gross margin above **23.8%**.

**Threats**
- **Valuation**: **28× earnings** for three years of declining EPS.
- Global competition from Siemens, ABB, Schneider, Eaton in large electrical infrastructure.
- Diluted exposure — appliances and general industrial motors damping the data centre effect.

- **The story and the results point in opposite directions (the central risk).** Orders are described as doubling and the power group grew **more than 30%** — yet **EPS has fallen for three consecutive years, from NT$2.77 to NT$2.42**, and **2026Q1 came in below the prior year**. At **28× earnings**, the market is paying for a conversion that has not yet occurred.
- **Growth is arriving at lower margin.** FY2025 revenue rose about **7%** while EPS fell roughly **11%**, and **gross margin has been flat at 23–25% for six quarters**. If data centre work is being won on price or carries heavy project costs, revenue growth will not produce proportional profit.
- **Capital efficiency.** **6.24% return on equity** on **NT$90.7bn of equity**. A large balance sheet earning single-digit returns is not obviously improved by adding more revenue at existing margins.
- **Dilution of exposure.** Appliances, air conditioning and general industrial motors are large parts of the business and grow slowly. Even strong data centre growth is damped in the consolidated result — which is precisely what the numbers show.
- **Execution and acquisition risk.** The **Dynaciate acquisition** must be integrated, and modular data centre delivery is a project business with execution risk very different from selling motors.
- **Timing.** US data centre contributions are expected **from 2027 at the earliest**. That is a long wait at a 28× multiple, and the guidance for FY2026 gross margin above 23.8% has yet to be demonstrated.

TECO's outlook is a single question: **when does the order book become profit?** The axes to watch:

- **Gross margin.** The decisive number. Flat at **23–25%** for six quarters, with management guiding **FY2026 above FY2025's 23.8%**. Any sustained move above that band would be the first hard evidence that the data centre mix is worth more than the old mix.
- **EPS breaking the downtrend.** **NT$2.77 → 2.73 → NT$2.42** across three years, with **2026Q1's NT$0.51 below NT$0.54**. A full year above NT$2.42 is the minimum required to justify a 28× multiple; anything less extends a three-year decline into a fourth.
- **Power and energy group growth and its share of the total.** Growing **more than 30%** — the question is whether it becomes large enough to move the consolidated result, or remains one segment among several.
- **Dynaciate integration and modular data centre orders.** Whether the acquisition produces contracted work in Southeast Asia, and at what margin.
- **The US pipeline.** Contribution expected **from 2027 at the earliest** — a milestone to verify rather than anticipate.

Bottom line: TECO has been making electric motors since **1956**, and the AI data centre build-out has given a seventy-year-old industrial company an unexpectedly relevant catalogue — **power distribution, transformers, switchgear and cooling** — with the **power group growing over 30%**, a **Malaysian acquisition for modular data centres**, and a chairman saying orders are doubling. It is also a company whose **EPS has fallen three years running to NT$2.42**, whose **gross margin has not moved in six quarters**, which earns **6.24% on NT$90.7bn of equity**, which **cut its dividend**, and which trades at **28× those declining earnings**. Judge it on **gross margin and full-year EPS** — the opportunity is real; the conversion is not yet visible.
